# The Other Half of the World

There is a place in the Atacama Desert where the sky does something most of us will never see. After sunset the light doesn't fade so much as deepen, and then the stars arrive — not a handful, not a polite scattering, but an abundance that feels almost like an emergency. The Milky Way does not look like a smudge. It looks like a river that has burst its banks, spilled across the entire dome of the sky, and gone running with light. Astronomers fight to protect this darkness. They build their telescopes on mountaintops above the last clean air, and they speak about night the way conservationists speak about rainforest — as a resource, ancient and vanishing, that we are burning through without noticing.

They are right, and it is stranger than they usually say. Night is not simply getting brighter. It is being dismantled.

For nearly the entire history of our species, night was a country people actually visited. Firelight was precious and small. A candle cost a day's wages in some centuries; even a rushlight was hoarded. When the sun went down, most of the world went with it, and the human body did what bodies had done for millions of years: it surrendered. But the surrender was not the long, sealed unconsciousness we now call "a good night's sleep." Historians reading diaries and court records from the centuries before electric light kept finding the same peculiar phrase: *first sleep*. And then, a few hours later, *second sleep*. Between them lay a quiet interval of an hour or two when people would get up in the dark — to pray, to talk, to visit a neighbor by the light of the moon, to make love, or simply to lie awake thinking, in a state one diarist described as uniquely suited to meditation. This was not insomnia. It was the normal architecture of human sleep, as regular as the beat of a heart. We did not sleep through the night until we lit it.

And what a lighting we gave it. In a single century — the one just past — we did to night what earlier ages did to forests. Cities now glow from space like embers. By one estimate, most people in North America and Europe cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. The stars have not gone anywhere. The sky has simply been pulled down over our eyes like a lid. We invented a term for this, "light pollution," and the term is too weak. Pollution suggests dirt, something to be scrubbed off. What we have done is more like a forgetting. We have produced a civilization that is, in the most literal sense, enlightened, and in exchange we have given up the dark that our minds grew up in.

Because the dark was not empty. It was the first gallery, the first storybook, the first cinema. Every mythology we have was rehearsed under a sky so crowded with stars that they demanded explaining: the hunter, the bear, the river of souls, the emu in the sky that Aboriginal Australians read in the dark rifts of the Milky Way itself. The night was where the dead went, where the gods walked, where dreams were sent from. It was also where the actual work of the imagination happened. Sleep, we now know, is when the brain files the day, washes out its debris, and rehearses futures. But even the waking dark had its uses. The hour between first sleep and second sleep was, one historian has suggested, where a great deal of the inner life of earlier centuries actually lived — the prayers, the doubts, the sudden resolutions, the conversations with oneself that daylight does not permit.

We have not replaced any of this. We have only canceled it. The last thing most people see at night is a screen, a rectangle of purchased light, and the first thing they see in the morning is another one. The dark in between is treated as a gap, an outage, a problem to be engineered away with blackout curtains and melatonin and white-noise machines. We speak of "getting" sleep the way we speak of getting gas — as a refueling, not a passage.

The cost is not only ours. Sea turtle hatchlings, born on the beach at night, instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the sea, moonlit and star-silvered. Now it often means a strip of hotels. They march inland, away from the ocean, toward their deaths in parking lots and pools. Moths, navigating by the moon as sailors once did, spiral into streetlights in a confusion that looks like madness and is actually a very old map failing. Migrating songbirds, by the billions, pass over continents that no longer go dark, and it scrambles the sky they steer by. Even the cells of our bodies keep a second clock, tuned to darkness, and we override it nightly with the flip of a switch — then wonder at the slow accumulation of ills that follow.

None of this is a call to blow out the lights and go back to the rushlight and the wolf. Darkness, for our ancestors, was also danger, and the fear of it was earned. It is a call to notice that night is not the absence of the world but the other half of it, and that we have been living in a permanently lit half-room of our own house, telling ourselves there is nothing in the rest.

There is a small ritual I would recommend, and it costs nothing. Go somewhere — a field, a coastline, a high desert, anywhere the towns are behind you — on a night with no moon. Wait. The eyes are slow; they take half an hour to open their full aperture, and every flash of a phone screen undoes minutes of the work. So wait, and do nothing, and let the dark arrive the way it used to. First the bright stars. Then the faint ones, in crowds. Then the Milky Way, if you are lucky, rising like weather. You will feel small, and then you will feel something better than small: continuous. The light you are looking at left its stars before there were people. Every human who ever lived looked up into this same darkness and made stories to live with it. The sky is the oldest thing we still have, and it is hanging above the parking lot, above the highway, above the town limits, exactly where it always was.

The night is not gone. It is only waiting, just past the edge of the light, for us to come out and remember it.

A candle cost a day's wages in some centuries; even a rushlight was hoarded. When the sun went down, most of the world went with it, and the human body did what bodies had done for millions of years: it surrendered. But the surrender was not the long, sealed unconsciousness we now call "a good night's sleep." Historians reading diaries and court records from the centuries before electric light kept finding the same peculiar phrase: first sleep. And then, a few hours later, second sleep. Between them lay a quiet interval of an hour or two when people would get up in the dark — to pray, to talk, to visit a neighbor by the light of the moon, to make love, or simply to lie awake thinking, in a state that one sixteenth-century diarist described as uniquely suited to meditation. This was not insomnia. It was the normal architecture of human sleep, as regular as the beat of a heart. We did not sleep through the night until we lit it.

And what a lighting we gave it. In a single century — the one just past — we did to night what earlier ages did to forests.Cities now glow from space like embers. Three quarters of North Americans and Europeans, by one estimate, cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. The stars have not gone anywhere. The sky has simply been pulled down over our eyes like a lid. We invented a term for this, "light pollution," and the term is too weak. Pollution suggests dirt, something to be scrubbed off. What we have done is more like a forgetting. We have produced a civilization that is, in the most literal sense, enlightened, and in exchange we have given up the dark that our minds grew up in.

Because the dark was not empty. It was the first gallery, the first storybook, the first cinema. Every mythology we have was rehearsed under a sky so crowded with stars that they demanded explaining: the hunter, the bear, the river of souls, the emu in the sky that Aboriginal Australians read in the dark rifts of the Milky Way itself. The night was where the dead went, where the gods walked, where dreams were sent from. It was also where the actual work of the imagination happened. Psychologists now suspect that the brain uses sleep to file the day, to wash out its accumulated debris, to rehearse threats and practice futures. But even the waking dark had its uses. The hour between first sleep and second sleep was, one historian has suggested, where a great deal of the inner life of earlier centuries actually lived — the prayers, the doubts, the sudden resolutions, the conversations with oneself that daylight does not permit.

We have not replaced any of this. We have only canceled it. The last thing most people see at night is a screen, a rectangle of purchased light, and the first thing they see in the morning is another one. The dark in between is treated as a gap, an outage, a problem to be engineered away with blackout curtains and melatonin and white-noise machines. We speak of "getting" sleep the way we speak of getting gas — as a refueling, not a passage.

The cost is not only ours. Sea turtle hatchlings, born on the beach at night, instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the sea, moonlit and star-silvered. Now it often means a strip of hotels. They march inland, away from the ocean, toward their deaths in parking lots and pools. Moths, navigating by the moon as sailors once did, spiral into streetlights in a confusion that looks like madness and is actually a very old map failing. Migrating birds, songbirds by the billions, pass over continents that no longer go dark, and it scrambles the sky they steer by. Even the cells of our bodies keep a second clock, tuned to darkness, and we override it nightly with the flip of a switch — then wonder at the slow, mysterious accumulation of ills that follow.

It is a call to notice that night is not the absence of the world but the other half of it, and that we have been living in a permanently lit half-room of our own house, telling ourselves there is nothing in the rest.

There is a small ritual I would recommend, and it costs nothing. Go somewhere — a field, a coastline, a high desert, anywhere the towns are behind you — on a night with no moon. Wait. This is the hard part, because the eyes are slow. They take half an hour to open their full aperture; every flash of a phone screen undoes minutes of the work. So wait, and do nothing, and let the dark arrive the way it used to. First the bright stars. Then the faint ones, in crowds. Then the Milky Way, if you are lucky, rising like weather. You will feel small, and then you will feel something better than small: continuous. The light you are looking at left its stars before there were people. Every human who ever lived, every one of them, looked up into this same darkness and made stories to live with it. The sky is the oldest thing we still have, and it is hanging above the parking lot, above the highway, above the town limits, exactly where it always was.

The night is not gone. It is only waiting, just past the edge of the light, for us to come out and remember it.
